questions.question: What is this?

model_named.detail: answered by Nemotron 3 Ultra

blocks.text: PYRION is a tool that ranks NASA PSI combustion investigations by how well they apply to a condition you set. The home page (the Envelope page) has three main panels: the controls on the left, the envelope chart in the middle, and the verdict panel on the right.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Controls panel: you set oxygen (% by volume), pressure (kPa), gravity regime, fuel phase, diluent, and flame type. Changing any control switches the view to "Your condition". You can also click a scenario tile to load a preset condition.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Envelope chart: plots oxygen vs pressure. Each shaded outline is the envelope of one regime — the oxygen and pressure range that PSI tested for that combination of gravity, fuel phase, diluent, and flame type. Your condition is the target marker. Inside an outline means a test covered that oxygen and pressure; outside means no extracted PSI test did.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Verdict panel: every investigation gets exactly one of four verdicts for your condition, decided by fixed rules. Applicable — your condition lies inside what the investigation tested in every respect you stated. Extrapolation — same regime but your numbers fall outside the tested region (with a distance level). Insufficient evidence — the extracted records do not say enough to place your condition. Not comparable (different regime) — gravity, fuel phase, diluent, or flame type differ; no distance is computed across that barrier.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Investigations are grouped into clusters by regime; the investigation's verdict is the best among its clusters (Applicable beats Extrapolation beats Insufficient evidence beats Not comparable). The right column "Where the evidence is" lists investigations that already apply and, for others, the smallest change to your condition that would make each one comparable. "Take me there" moves your condition to that point.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

questions.question: What is the column on the right?

model_named.detail: answered by Nemotron 3 Ultra

blocks.text: The column on the right is the **NAVIGATOR** panel ("Where the evidence is"). It shows every investigation in PSI and, for each one that isn't already *Applicable* to your current condition, the smallest change you could make to your condition so that investigation would become comparable. Each row has a "Take me there" button that moves your condition to that point and re-runs the verdict. Investigations that already apply are listed at the top; those with no possible route (for example, missing gravity regime in the records) appear under "No route found".
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

questions.question: ¿Por qué algunas investigaciones salen en gris?

model_named.detail: answered by Nemotron 3 Ultra

blocks.text:
En PYRION, las investigaciones aparecen en gris cuando su **veredicto es "insufficient evidence"** (evidencia insuficiente). Esto significa que la investigación existe en la base de datos PSI, pero **no tiene datos extraídos** (por ejemplo, límites de inflamabilidad, velocidades de propagación, etc.) que el motor pueda comparar con tu condición actual. Por tanto, el motor no puede emitir un veredicto de "applicable", "extrapolation" ni "not comparable"; solo sabe que la investigación está ahí, pero no tiene números para trabajar.

En el panel "Where the evidence is" (segunda tarjeta de la columna derecha) verás estas investigaciones agrupadas bajo **"No route found"** con la razón "No extracted data". No hay una ruta (pequeño cambio en O₂, presión o gravedad) que las haga comparables, porque les faltan los datos numéricos necesarios.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

questions.question: Why do flames spread differently in microgravity?

model_named.detail: answered by google/gemma-4-31b-it (fell back from Nemotron 3 Ultra)

blocks.text: Gravity significantly influences flames through density gradients. On Earth, the large temperature difference between the flame and ambient gas creates a density gradient that induces a strong velocity field, causing flames to lift, point upward, and flicker.
blocks.label: NASA source — quote checked on the cited page

citations.quote: To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the density gradients in flames... The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward.
citations.title: PSI-20 ACME BRE - Science Documents: ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity

blocks.text: In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy fundamentally changes how combustion occurs. Without gravity, the density-driven convection that pulls fresh oxygen into the flame and pushes exhaust gases away is suppressed. Consequently, the transport of reactants and products relies almost entirely on molecular diffusion, which is much slower than convection. This typically results in spherical flame shapes and slower spread rates, as the flame must wait for oxygen to diffuse through the combustion products to reach the fuel surface. This lack of buoyancy also removes the 'flicker' and upward orientation seen in terrestrial fires.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

questions.question: Why does oxygen partial pressure matter more than the oxygen percentage?

model_named.detail: answered by google/gemma-4-31b-it (fell back from Nemotron 3 Ultra)

blocks.text:
Oxygen partial pressure is a more critical driver of flammability than percentage because it represents the actual number of oxygen molecules available in a given volume to react with fuel. 

Combustion is a chemical reaction that depends on the collision frequency between fuel and oxidizer molecules. While the oxygen percentage tells you the ratio of oxygen to other gases, the partial pressure tells you the absolute density of those oxygen molecules. For example, [number removed: not from a source]% oxygen at [number removed: not from a source] psia provides far fewer oxygen molecules per cubic centimeter than [number removed: not from a source]% oxygen at [number removed: not from a source] psia. If the partial pressure drops too low, there are not enough collisions to sustain the chain reaction, and the flame will extinguish, regardless of the percentage. 

This is why we track both: the percentage often defines the chemical regime, but the total pressure scales the actual availability of the reactant. In reduced-pressure environments, you must increase the oxygen percentage just to maintain the same partial pressure required for human respiration or material ignition.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Human physiology and atmospheric design must account for this relationship, as a lower total cabin pressure requires a higher oxygen percentage to maintain the necessary partial pressure for lung function.
blocks.label: NASA source — quote checked on the cited page

citations.quote: A lower cabin total pressure must contain a higher percentage of O2 to sustain a given O2 partial pressure within the lungs.
citations.title: NESC, Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on ECLSS, NASA/TM-20260003925

questions.question: What is the difference between upward and downward flame spread?

model_named.detail: answered by google/gemma-4-31b-it (fell back from Nemotron 3 Ultra)

blocks.text: The primary difference between upward and downward flame spread is the role of buoyancy. In upward spread, the hot combustion gases are buoyant and rise, which preheats the fuel above the flame front and delivers fresh oxygen to the reaction zone. This positive feedback loop typically accelerates the spread rate. In downward spread, buoyancy works against the direction of propagation; hot gases rise away from the unburnt fuel, reducing the preheating effect and generally resulting in a slower spread rate compared to the upward configuration. In microgravity, where buoyancy is absent, this directional distinction disappears.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Upward flame spread is noted for its complexity in modeling because the process is non-steady and the flame size increases rapidly.
blocks.label: NASA source — quote checked on the cited page

citations.quote: While flame spread in the upward configuration is closely related to fire safety studies, it is also quite complex to model because the flame spread process is not steady and the flame size quickly becomes very large.
citations.title: PSI-25 BASS-II - Reports: BASS-II Summary Report

questions.question: ¿Por qué la llama de una vela es esférica en microgravedad?

model_named.detail: answered by google/gemma-4-31b-it (fell back from Nemotron 3 Ultra)

blocks.text: En la Tierra, el aire caliente producido por la llama es menos denso que el aire frío circundante, lo que genera una fuerza de flotabilidad (convección) que empuja los gases hacia arriba, creando la forma alargada característica. En microgravedad, la flotabilidad desaparece porque no hay una diferencia de densidad impulsada por la gravedad. Sin convección, el combustible y el oxígeno se mueven únicamente mediante difusión molecular, que ocurre uniformemente en todas las direcciones desde el centro de la reacción, resultando en una llama esférica. Este proceso es mucho más lento, lo que reduce la tasa de combustión y hace que la llama sea menos luminosa.
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

blocks.text: Experimentos en la estación Mir demostraron que las llamas de velas pueden sostenerse en microgravedad basándose únicamente en el transporte difusivo, aunque con una tasa de combustión mucho menor que en la Tierra.
blocks.label: NASA source — quote checked on the cited page

citations.quote: in the absence of convection, a steady flame could not exist; diffusive transport alone could not sustain a flame. Two spaceflight experiments demonstrated conclusively the fallacy of such arguments.
citations.title: PSI-20 ACME BRE - Science Documents: ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity

questions.question: ¿Qué es el límite de oxígeno de un material?

model_named.detail: answered by google/gemma-4-31b-it (fell back from Nemotron 3 Ultra)

blocks.text:
El límite de oxígeno de un material, comúnmente referido como el Índice Límite de Oxígeno (LOC por sus siglas en inglés, Limiting Oxygen Concentration), es la concentración mínima de oxígeno en una mezcla gaseosa (generalmente oxígeno y un gas inerte como el nitrógeno) necesaria para que un material soporte la combustión. 

Desde la perspectiva de la física de la combustión, este valor es crítico porque determina si un material es inflamable bajo condiciones atmosféricas específicas. Si la concentración de oxígeno en la cabina es inferior al LOC del material, el fuego no puede mantenerse. Factores como la presión total y la gravedad afectan este límite; por ejemplo, en microgravedad, la ausencia de convección natural altera la difusión del oxígeno hacia la llama, lo que puede modificar la inflamabilidad del material en comparación con los resultados obtenidos en Tierra ([number removed: not from a source]-g).
blocks.label: TARS expert knowledge — not verified against a source

questions.question: What does FM2 plan to test, and at which atmospheres?

model_named.detail: answered by Nemotron 3 Ultra

blocks.text: FM2 (Flammability of Materials on the Moon) will conduct the first-ever combustion experiment on another planetary body, testing material flammability on the lunar surface at 1/[number removed: not from a source] g. The experiment will find the flammability limit of one material per flight at 8.2 psia upward burning, obtain data on ignition, flame growth, extinction oxygen levels, and flame spread over solid materials in lunar gravity, and compare results to 1-g tests.
blocks.label: NASA source — quote checked on the cited page

Conduct Lunar surface flammability tests that are important to NASA HLS (Human Landing System).
B.  Conduct test to assist in validation of the Phase 3 testing in support of HLS and NESC program; Find 
flammability limit of 1 material per flight at 8.2 psia upward burning.
citations.title: Ferkul et al., Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC 2026 (NTRS 20260001966)

citations.doc_id: nasa/ntrs-20260001966/Ferkul-Lunar and Planetary Science Conf 2026 v2.pdf

materials in Lunar gravity and compare to 1-g results.

blocks.text: FM2 plans four tests, each at 8.2 psia total pressure with different oxygen concentrations: Test 1 at 37% O2, Test 2 at 33% O2, Test 3 at 29% O2, and Test 4 at 25% O2, balance nitrogen. The fuel is Synergy Pro "Navy" fabric sheets mounted between thin metal frames, exposing 2 cm x 20 cm of both sides, ignited by a hot wire at the bottom for upward burns.

Test 2: 8.2 psia (+/- 0.3 psi), 33% O2 , balance nitrogen)
Test 3: 8.2 psia (+/- 0.3 psi), 29% O2 , balance nitrogen)
Test 4: 8.2 psia (+/- 0.3 psi), 25% O2 , balance nitrogen)

blocks.text: FM2 is designed to bridge the gap between NASA's current 1-g upward flame spread test (Test 1) and actual material behavior in lunar gravity. The four oxygen concentrations (37%, 33%, 29%, 25% at 8.2 psia) span a range expected to bracket the lunar oxygen limit of flammability for the selected fabric. Testing at 8.2 psia matches the planned exploration atmosphere for the Human Landing System.
